URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) Report for the Academic Year 2022-2023 Introduction The URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) has been engaged in several important topics over the course of the academic year. These topics included the review of overhead funds on research, the expansion of the committee to better represent the interests of research faculty, and the impact of university policies on the research environment. Review of Overhead Expenditures, Administration, and Policies During the academic year 2022-2023, the URI Faculty Senate Committee on Research and Creative Activities reviewed the research overhead funds collected and spent across the colleges. The committee found that while research expenditures at URI have significantly increased over the past decade, the effective percentage of overhead dollars generated by that research decreased. The graph below shows the trend in the research expenditures at URI over the past decade: Source: URI Institutional Research, John Stringer (2023)

The effective indirect cost collected on research expenditures for FY 2022 was only 19.1% compared to the official rate of 57.5%.
This is a concern that needs attention.
The committee identified several potential reasons why the effective indirect rate is so much smaller than the official rate.
These include the fact that the indirect costs collected from state funds are only 25% and have stayed the same over decades, cost-sharing that may be required on some federal grants, or grant funds from foundations may restrict the percentage of the overhead that could be collected.
Grants for scholarships generally do not provide overhead.
Regardless, the net effect is less overhead dollars available to be returned to the PIs, their departments, and colleges and to support new research initiatives at URI.
During the inspection of the actual indirect cost expenditures, the committee discovered that an associate vice president for facilities was hired with 100% of their salary and fringe being charged to indirect cost, which is out of line with the expectation that overhead for research should be used to support research.

Additionally, there needs to be more transparency on how the division of administration and finance spends the portion of the indirect costs they receive.
By comparison, the division of research is severely underfunded to provide services to the faculty in writing and submitting grant proposals and managing the submission and successful and expeditious establishment of funded grant accounts.
PIs, colleges, and departments report that they are also underfunded to support research activities and investment in growing funded research portfolios.
It is difficult to understand why URI is spending so much on administration and finance from research overhead dollars and not enough on the direct support of the researchers that generate those overhead dollars through their hard work.
The committee encourages a conversation with President Parlange to change the policies for the distribution of overhead.
More favorable overhead distribution to the faculty who generate it will empower the research faculty to be even more productive in grantsmanship and expand the number of faculty engaged in funded research.

These changes will directly align with the URI strategic plan to increase research productivity.
Additionally, the committee spent significant time reviewing how overhead funds on research are collected and spent among colleges at URI.
We found that the current process needs to be standardized across all colleges, and there are discrepancies in how funds are allocated.
For example, some colleges allocate more overhead funds to the principal investigator (PI), while others allocate more to the college or department.
We recommend that the university develop a more transparent process for indirect cost waivers and allocation of overhead funds to ensure

they are used effectively and efficiently to support research efforts.
This process should consider the needs of the PIs, departments, and colleges and the requirements of funding agencies.
Overall, the committee urges the university to prioritize the direct support of research faculty and activities by allocating a higher percentage of overhead funds to support these efforts.
By doing so, URI can maximize its research productivity and achieve greater success in securing external funding.
Expansion of the Committee on Research: The committee considered expanding its membership to better represent the interests and concerns of the research faculty at URI.
We regularly recruit expert researchers to help with the review of grant proposals.
We propose adding non-senators to the Research and Creative Activities Committee.
This expansion will enable the committee to serve the needs of the research community at URI.

Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE) Charge: The Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE), an expanded URI Research and Creative Activities Committee, is charged with representing and advocating for the research and and creative activities community at URI.
The committee shall consist of six senators and six non-senator members of the faculty who are actively engaged in research and creative activities.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall serve as an ex officio member of the committee.
The committee is responsible for addressing the concerns and needs of the research and creative activities community and recommending policies and practices that will support and enhance research and creative activities at URI.
Membership: The committee shall consist of six senators appointed by the President of the Faculty Senate and six members of the research faculty appointed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
Members shall be selected based on their active engagement in research and creative activities and shall represent a diversity of disciplines and areas of expertise.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall serve as an ex officio member of the committee.

The committee shall be chaired by one of the senators appointed by the Faculty Senate President.
The committee will also work closely with the Vice President for Research and Economic Development to ensure alignment with university policies and goals related to research and creative activities.
The committee will meet at least once per semester or more often as needed to discuss matters related to research and creative activities at URI.
Adding experienced and engaged research faculty to the committee will help ensure that the voices and concerns of those actively engaged in research activities are represented and heard.
Meetings: The committee shall meet at least once per semester or more often as needed.
Meetings may be conducted in person or remotely, as determined by the committee chair.
Meetings shall be open to all members of the URI community, and minutes shall be kept and made available to the public.
Responsibilities: The committee shall have the following responsibilities: 1.
Represent and advocate for the research and creative activities at URI. 2.
Address the concerns and needs of the faculty engaged in research and creative activities. 3.

Review and evaluate the effectiveness of policies and practices related to research and creative activities. 4.
Recommend policies and practices to support and enhance URI's research and creative activities. 5.
Promote collaboration and communication among researchers and creative practitioners across disciplines and colleges. 6.
Advise the Vice President for Research and Economic Development on matters related to research and creative activities. 7.
Provide feedback and input on proposals and initiatives related to research and creative activities. 8.
Collaborate with other committees and organizations at URI to promote and support research and creative activities.

9.
Submit an annual report to the Faculty Senate summarizing the committee's activities and accomplishments over the past academic year.
Impact of University Policies on the Research Environment Some recent policies at URI have negatively impacted the faculty's research and creative activities.
One example is the drone policy which has caused many problems for faculty in their creative work.
Drones are used by faculty in a variety of ways, such as surveying, videography, construction, transportation, the design of new types of drones, software engineering for drones, and AI and drones, among others.
However, the current drone policy needs to consider the real faculty research needs and applications and has become an obstacle.
We recommend that the policy be revised to accommodate faculty needs better.
The IT department's push to take administrative control of faculty computers has caused considerable frustration, concerns, and damage to the research efforts of faculty.
In addition to the drone policy, three IT policies were implemented during the summer of 2022, which have caused chaos and havoc for faculty researchers since December 2022.

These policies were implemented without proper consultation with faculty, leading to a lack of understanding and an inability to comply with the new policies.
We support the review of the three IT policies by the Faculty Senate Committee on Technology and Infrastructure (CTI).
CTI has correctly identified some of the deficiencies and problems with those policies.
In particular, it should be noted that faculty own the intellectual property of research, creative works, and teaching materials stored on their computers.
The university may own the hardware, but they do not own the faculty’s intellectual and personal data stored on those computers.
Faculty members have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their computers, as they contain sensitive and personal information, research data, and intellectual property.
The IT policy infringes upon this right by allowing administrative access to faculty computers without just cause or consent.
Other policies that continue to be of concern and interfere with research activities include purchasing, travel, and hiring graduate students, postdocs, and faculty.

These long-standing issues require a new effort to review and revise these policies to support faculty research efforts better.
The newly proposed committee, CURE, can be central to these reviews and policy revisions.
By bringing together research faculty and administrators, URI can work towards improving policies and procedures to better support the research and creative activities of the faculty.
We recommend that the CURE committee be given the resources and authority to conduct a comprehensive review of these policies and to make recommendations for necessary revisions.

Summary of recommendations Summary of recommendations from the URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) Report for the Academic Year 2022-2023: 1.
The university needs to prioritize the direct support of research faculty and activities by allocating a higher percentage of overhead funds to support these efforts.
The policies for the overhead distribution need to be changed to provide more favorable overhead distribution to the faculty who generate it. 2.
The university needs to develop a more transparent process for indirect cost waivers and allocation of overhead funds to ensure they are used effectively and efficiently to support research efforts.
This process should consider the needs of the PIs, departments, and colleges and the requirements of funding agencies. 3.
The Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE) should be created to better represent the interests and concerns of the research faculty at URI.
This expansion of CRCA will serve the needs of the research community at URI. 4.
The drone policy needs to be revised to accommodate faculty needs better. 5.

The three IT policies implemented during the summer of 2022 have caused chaos and havoc for faculty researchers since December 2022.
The policies need to be carefully reviewed by the Faculty Senate Committee on Technology and Infrastructure (CTI), and necessary revisions should be made. 6.
Purchasing, travel, and hiring graduate students, postdocs, and faculty policies need to be reviewed and revised to support faculty research efforts better. 7.
The newly proposed committee, CURE, should be given the resources and authority to conduct a comprehensive review of policies related to research and creative activities and make recommendations for necessary revisions.
Overall, the committee urges the university to prioritize the support of research and creative activities to maximize its research productivity and achieve greater success in securing external funding.

Conclusion The URI Faculty Senate Committee on Research and Creative Activities has been working diligently to support the research community at URI. Our efforts to review overhead funds, expand the committee, and examine university policies have been valuable in identifying areas for improvement and ensuring that researchers at URI have the support they need to be successful. We will continue to work on these issues and look forward to making further progress in the coming academic year. Respectfully submitted, Sen. Bahram Nassersharif, Chair, and FSEC Liaison Sen. Expansion of CRCA Membership: The CRCA expanded its membership to include five new research-active, non-senator voting members and added the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex-officio non-voting member.
This change aims to diversify perspectives within the committee, increase representation from various disciplines, and strengthen links to current research challenges and the university administration. 2.
Review of Indirect Cost Expenditures: The report analyzed the FY2023 overhead expenses, revealing a substantial gap between expected indirect cost recovery and the actual overhead revenue allocation.

Suggestions for improvement include optimizing the indirect cost recovery process, developing a transparent methodology for allocating indirect costs and enhancing detailed reporting and monitoring to improve transparency and strategic investment. 3.
Analysis of the Office of Research Operations: The operational review highlighted underfunding and staffing issues in the Office of Research Development (ORD), retention challenges, and the need for improved support for faculty in research activities.
Recommendations include hiring new positions as suggested by both a faculty survey and an external review and reevaluating the centralization of research support. 4.
Issues in Sponsored Research Operations: Challenges in managing larger, multi- institutional projects and bottlenecks in IRB reviews were identified as reducing productivity.
Recommendations focus on improving staffing levels and response times in the Office of Sponsored Research (OSP) to enhance research productivity. 5.
Impact of ITS Operations on Research: The current IT policies were evaluated for their impact on research productivity.
Recommendations include creating

streamlined services for software installation requests and providing guidelines for data backup prior to the installation of monitoring software. 6.
Conclusions and Recommendations: The report concludes by summarizing the significant findings and reiterating critical recommendations.
It emphasizes the need for enhanced communication and collaboration across departments and improved policy development to align with the university’s strategic objectives.
II.
Introduction The Annual Report of the CRCA for the year 2024 documents the pivotal advancements and sustained efforts in reinforcing the research and creative endeavors at the University of Rhode Island (URI).
This report, prepared by a dedicated team led by Sen.
Bahram Nassersharif, Acting Chair, underlines the critical activities and strategic initiatives undertaken by the CRCA to cultivate a robust research culture at the university.
The CRCA's responsibilities, deeply embedded in URI's academic fabric as delineated in Appendix C of the URI University Manual, encompass a broad spectrum of functions.

These include advocating for and supporting the diverse spectrum of research and creative activities that define the scholarly community at URI.
The committee acts as an essential bridge between the university administration and its vibrant intellectual community, advising on policies, supporting infrastructure needs, and fostering an environment conducive to cutting- edge research and innovation.
This year's report highlights several key developments including the strategic expansion of the committee’s membership, aimed at enhancing the diversity of perspectives and bolstering the representation from various academic disciplines.
Such changes are designed not only to enrich the committee's deliberations but also to align closely with the university's strategic goals of fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and responsiveness to emerging research challenges.
Through a detailed account of the CRCA's operations, this introduction sets the stage for a comprehensive understanding of the committee’s objectives, challenges, and the substantial impact of its work on the university’s broader strategic ambitions.

This narrative provides a contextual backdrop for the discussions and recommendations that follow in the subsequent sections of this report.
The mandates of the CRCA, as outlined in Appendix C of the URI University Manual, highlight its comprehensive responsibilities and functions:

CRCA Charges ● Advocacy and Support for Research and Creative Activities: The CRCA is tasked with promoting a comprehensive understanding of research, creative, and scholarly work.
This includes enhancing the overall well-being of such activities at URI by identifying and addressing challenges that hinder these efforts.
The committee provides recommendations for improving the management of research affairs and acts as an advisory body to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development. ● Library and Open Access: Acting as a liaison between the University Library and the faculty, the CRCA advises on matters of general faculty concern regarding the library.
It plays a consultative role in assessing the library's long-range needs and the adequacy of its budget and advises on the implementation and interpretation of URI’s Open-Access Policy.
This includes resolving disputes concerning the policy and recommending changes to the Faculty Senate. ● Competitive Grants Subcommittee: This subcommittee of the CRCA solicits proposals from faculty and awards financial support on a competitive basis for faculty development and proposal development programs.

These programs support various faculty needs, including salaries, fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment. ● Center Review Subcommittee: Responsible for reviewing applications for new centers and institutes as well as the continuing authorization of existing ones.
This subcommittee ensures that such entities meet their goals and contribute effectively to the university’s research environment.
III.
Expansion of CRCA Membership CRCA plays a crucial role in shaping the institution's research policies, fostering an environment that supports scholarly endeavors, and ensuring the distribution of research-related resources effectively aligns with the university's strategic goals.
The recent changes made in the Senate, specifically expanding the committee's membership to include five new research-active but non-senator voting members, as well as adding the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex officio non-voting member, have significant implications for the governance of research at URI.

Rationale for Expanded Membership ● Enhanced Diversity of Perspectives: By incorporating five new research- active but non-senator members, the committee benefits from a broader range of insights and experiences.
These members, being active researchers, bring a fresh, on-the-ground perspective that can contribute to more informed and effective decision-making regarding research policies and resource allocation.

● Increased Representation from Various Disciplines: Research-active members likely come from diverse academic backgrounds and disciplines.
This variety ensures that the unique needs and challenges of different research areas are understood and considered, leading to more comprehensive and inclusive research policies. ● Direct Link to Current Research Challenges: Active researchers are more likely to be aware of the latest trends, challenges, and opportunities in research, including funding, technology, and interdisciplinary collaboration.
Their contributions can help the committee stay relevant and responsive to the evolving research landscape. ● Strengthening Research Culture: Including members who are directly engaged in research activities can enhance the committee’s role in advocating for a robust research culture.
This can lead to more effective strategies to foster research and creative activities across the university. ● Connection with University Administration: The addition of the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex officio member provides a direct link to the university’s senior administration.

This connection can facilitate smoother implementation of committee decisions and better alignment of research initiatives with the university’s strategic objectives.
Expected Impacts from This Change ● Improved Policy Development: With inputs from diverse and active researchers, the committee is likely to develop policies that are more attuned to the actual needs of the research community.
This can lead to more effective use of resources and better support for cutting-edge research activities. ● Enhanced Communication and Collaboration: The presence of a wider range of members, especially the inclusion of a high-ranking administrative officer like the Vice President, can improve communication between researchers and the university administration.

This could lead to more collaborative efforts across departments and disciplines. ● Greater Advocacy for Research Needs: The expanded membership can strengthen the committee’s ability to advocate for the needs of the research community, potentially leading to enhanced support from the university in terms of funding, infrastructure, and administrative assistance. ● More Informed Decision Making: The direct involvement of active researchers ensures that the committee's decisions are informed by up-to- date knowledge of the research environment, technology advancements, and the global research agenda. ● Broader Impact on University Strategy: With strategic inputs from diverse academic fields and a direct link to university administration, the committee’s influence on the overall university strategy could increase,

aligning more closely with national and international research priorities and funding landscapes.
Going forward, these changes are expected to dynamically enhance the functionality and impact of the Committee on Research and Creative Activities at URI, fostering a more vibrant, responsive, and interdisciplinary research environment that aligns with both the academic and practical needs of the university.
This, in turn, should bolster URI's reputation as a leading research institution.
IV.
Review of Indirect Cost Expenditures Based on the information provided in the FY2023 Overhead Report, here is an analysis of the indirect cost report and suggestions for improvements: 1.
Indirect cost recovery comparison: ○ URI reported $108,622,286 in research expenditures during 2022- 2023. ○ At an indirect cost rate of 57.5%, the expected indirect cost recovery should be approximately $62,457,814 ($108,622,286 x 0.575). ○ The actual overhead revenue allocation reported in the document is $16,028,277. ○ There is a significant gap between the expected indirect cost recovery and the actual overhead revenue allocation, indicating that URI may not be fully recovering its indirect costs. 2.

Allocation of indirect costs: ○ The report did not provide a breakdown of the indirect cost distribution. ○ It is unclear from the report how these allocations are determined and whether they align with the actual overhead distribution formulas. 3.
Transparency and detail: ○ The report provides a high-level summary of indirect cost allocations and expenditures but lacks detailed breakdowns for some units. ○ Increasing transparency by providing more granular information on how indirect costs are spent particularly by the Division of Research and the Division of Finance and Administration. 4.
Strategic investment of indirect cost recovery: ○ The report indicates that a significant portion of indirect cost recovery is used for payroll and fringe benefits.
However, no additional information is provided as to who is being paid from overhead funds. ○ URI should consider strategically investing a portion of the indirect cost recovery in initiatives that support and enhance research activities, such as infrastructure improvements, seed funding for new projects, or direct support of faculty who generate overhead. 5.
Monitoring and analysis:

○ URI should regularly monitor and analyze its overhead expenditures to identify trends, variances, and opportunities for improvement. ○ Comparing actual indirect cost recovery against budgeted amounts and benchmarking against peer institutions can provide valuable insights.
Suggestions for improvement: 1.
Review and optimize the indirect cost recovery process to ensure that URI is capturing all eligible indirect costs associated with research activities. 2.
Under the New Budget Model, develop a transparent methodology for allocating indirect costs to administrative units based on their contribution to research support and directly to faculty who generate that indirect cost. 3.
Provide more detailed reporting on indirect cost utilization within each unit to enhance transparency and accountability. 4.
Implement regular monitoring and analysis of indirect cost recovery to identify trends, variances, and opportunities for improvement.
By addressing these areas, URI can improve its indirect cost recovery, ensure transparent allocation of funds, and strategically invest in research support and enhancement initiatives.
V.
Analysis of the Office of Research Operations ● A.

Operational Review ○ The committee discussed the research division’s administrative and operational efficiency. ○ Office of Research Development ■ ORD is currently under-funded and under-resourced.
There are retention issues, with very high turnover, as well as a need to hire new positions.
The committee acknowledges that the President and interim VPR are aware of the situation. ■ A survey of faculty perceptions of research support was conducted under former VPR Peter Snyder.
The Committee does not have access to the original survey but met with Melissa McCarthy to discuss the questions and outcomes.
The main finding was the need for more research support staff. ■ An external review was conducted in 2021 by the National Organization of Research Development’s (NORDP) Program for External Evaluation of Research Development (PEERD).
The committee received a copy of this report in mid-April.
The report recommends greater investment in research support and increased staffing, stating, “We strongly suggest URI consider

structural and staffing changes to [ORD] to strengthen its centralized role in the research enterprise.” ■ Individualized help with research development (e.g. grant proposals) is often not available to faculty when they need it. ■ Significant concerns exist about the new practice of hiring full- time remote staff who are not located near URI, such as the new AVP for Research. ○ Institutional Review Board ■ There are currently long delays with IRB review, with decision making sporadic and difficult to understand.
In some cases this has led to missed deadlines, and projects needing to be changed or moved outside of URI. ■ There are concerns that IRB reviewers do not have the necessary background to make decisions. ■ The committee wanted to investigate this further by inviting the IRB staff or VPR to join a committee meeting.
Recommend that the CRCA continue to investigate this issue. ○ Pre-award to Post-award process ■ This process is severely challenging for faculty.
Funds are difficult to locate.
There are many issues with different number codes being used to track awards and not cross-linked.

Pre- award is managed by the Research office; Post-award is managed by the Controller. ○ Centralization and Decentralization of research support ■ Many colleges have their own support staff for writing grant proposals.
The committee took steps towards gathering information about research staff in individual colleges and discussed whether research support should remain centralized under IBB. ● B.
Challenges and Opportunities Challenges: 1.
Underfunding and Resource Allocation: ● The Office of Research Development (ORD) faces significant challenges due to inadequate funding levels, which impede the office's ability to support research initiatives adequately. 2.
Staffing Issues and High Turnover: ● The ORD has been experiencing high staff turnover, leading to instability within the department.
